explanation:
[FEATURE: hr]
[EFFECT] Hour of day has a strongly non-monotonic, double-peaked effect. Contributions are deeply negative in the early morning hours (hitting their lowest point at 4 a.m.), turn positive from around 7 a.m. onwards, and reach two clear peaks: one at 8 a.m. (morning commute) and the highest one at 5 p.m. (evening commute). Late-night hours (after 10 p.m.) dip back into negative territory.
[IMPORTANCE] This is by far the most influential feature — ranked 1st with an importance score of 0.889, more than three times larger than the next feature. Getting the time of day right is the single most important factor in the model's prediction.

---

[FEATURE: temp]
[EFFECT] Temperature has a mostly upward, then slightly declining effect. Demand is strongly suppressed at very cold temperatures (near 0 °C) and rises steadily as conditions warm up, peaking around a normalised value of 0.74–0.76 (roughly 30–31 °C). At the very hottest extreme (near 40 °C) the contribution dips slightly back into negative territory, suggesting extreme heat mildly discourages rentals.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked 2nd with an importance of 0.253, temperature is the second-strongest driver of demand — a significant effect, though well below that of hour.

---

[FEATURE: yr]
[EFFECT] This is a simple step change between the two years in the data. The model assigns a negative contribution in 2011 and a positive one in 2012, reflecting that overall ridership grew substantially from one year to the next.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked 3rd with an importance of 0.217, year captures the system's overall growth trend and is the third-most influential feature — nearly as strong as temperature.

---

[FEATURE: mnth]
[EFFECT] Month has a non-monotonic seasonal pattern. January and February carry the largest negative contributions (around −0.21 to −0.24), demand rises through spring and summer to near-neutral, then reaches its highest point in October (+0.17), with September and November also positive. December is mildly positive. The autumn months are clearly the model's seasonal sweet spot.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked 4th with an importance of 0.086, month adds a meaningful but moderate seasonal layer on top of temperature.

---

[FEATURE: hum]
[EFFECT] At moderate humidity levels (roughly 10%–65%) the contribution is near-flat and slightly positive, meaning humidity in this range has little practical impact. As humidity climbs above about 65–70%, the contribution turns progressively negative, suppressing demand, reaching around −0.26 at near-100% humidity. Extreme low humidity (below ~7%) also shows a very negative contribution, though this appears at rare, unusual hours.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked 5th with an importance of 0.083 — a modest but real effect, mainly relevant at the high end of the humidity scale.

---

[FEATURE: weathersit]
[EFFECT] Weather situation works as a step-down scale. Clear weather (category 1) gives a small positive boost (+0.047). Mist or clouds (category 2) is nearly neutral (−0.002). Light rain or snow (category 3) produces a clear negative contribution (−0.349). Heavy rain (category 4) is also negative (−0.264), though somewhat less so than light rain, likely because heavy-rain hours are rare in the data.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked 6th with an importance of 0.061 — a meaningful effect when bad weather occurs, but less influential overall than temperature or season.

---

[FEATURE: weekday]
[EFFECT] The effect of day of the week is small across the board. Sunday carries the only clearly negative contribution (−0.065), weekdays Wednesday through Friday are slightly positive (up to +0.041 on Friday), and Saturday sits in between (+0.020). The total spread across all days is only about 0.10 log units.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked 7th with an importance of 0.024 — a minor influence. Day of week barely moves the needle compared to hour, temperature, or season.

---

[FEATURE: windspeed]
[EFFECT] At low to moderate wind speeds, the contribution is near zero and roughly flat. Above approximately 0.44 normalised (roughly 29 km/h), contributions turn increasingly negative, reaching around −0.34 at the highest observed wind speeds (~55 km/h). The effect is essentially negligible at calm conditions and only meaningful at high winds.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked 8th with an importance of 0.014 — a small effect, relevant only when winds are notably high.

---

[FEATURE: holiday]
[EFFECT] This is a near-negligible step change. Non-holiday hours have a contribution of essentially zero (+0.004), while public holiday hours carry a mild negative contribution (−0.145), meaning holidays slightly reduce predicted demand compared to a regular day.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked last (9th) with an importance of 0.008 — the weakest feature in the model by a clear margin. Its effect is negligible for most practical purposes.

---

[RECOMMENDATION] Operational planning should be driven primarily by **time of day** and **temperature**: concentrate bike and staff resources around the 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. commuter peaks, and scale overall fleet availability up during warm weather (roughly 20–31 °C) while reducing it during cold snaps or heatwaves. Secondary adjustments for rain, season, and humidity can further refine scheduling, but day of week and holiday status need only minor attention.
